title: When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain

Abstract Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with under-specified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong
answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the
missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that
recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk , an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information
Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to
ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a
smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain Yunxiang Li Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China Email: yli@se.cuhk.edu.hk Xixin Wu Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China Helen Meng Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China Abstract Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with under-specified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk , an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Clarification resolves a missing slot. The underspecified query admits two plausible year-specific answers. A standard LLM answers immediately and combines them incorrectly, whereas CIGAsk learns when to clarify through the asymmetric reward and how to ask through CIG, recovering the intended year and the correct answer in one turn. Figure 2: CIGAsk overview. (a) A trainable policy π θ \pi_{\theta} interacts with a fixed user simulator with oracle access to the latent intent q ∗ q^{*} , optionally requests clarification, and then produces a terminal answer. (b) CIG compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under the real history h ≤ t h_{\leq t} and the response-ablated history h ≤ t ∖ u t h_{\leq t}\setminus u_{t} using the same frozen reference policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , providing local credit for how to clarify. The outcome reward and Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus provide terminal credit for answer quality and when to clarify. After separate normalization, the intrinsic and outcome streams are combined into A ^ i , t CIG \hat{A}^{\mathrm{CIG}}_{i,t} for the GRPO update. Instruction-tuned LLMs ( Yang et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) achieve strong single-turn performance on QA benchmarks. Yet when a request is under-specified, as in “What was the operating loss carryforward amount?” for a table that lists both 2018 and 2019 figures ( Deng et al., 2022 ) , the same models often commit to one interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing a plausible but potentially incorrect answer without acknowledging the ambiguity. The failure is easy to demonstrate, can be costly in deployment, and is hard to remove with prompting alone. Addressing this failure requires the policy to learn two coupled skills in one training loop: when to ask rather than answer, and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating fact. Existing approaches address parts of this problem, but each has a limitation (§ 2 ). SFT-based self- training ( Andukuri et al., 2024 ) filters trajectories by outcome reward and lacks a per-turn signal that grades how effectively a clarification elicits the missing fact. Offline action-preference learning ( Chen et al., 2025 ) cannot adapt to the policy’s evolving trajectories. Rubric-guided RLVR ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) needs per-instance rubric annotation that does not scale. Privileged-critic RL ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) requires privileged side information during training. None of these recipes combines a signal for when to ask with per-turn credit for how to ask using only the supervision already available in the training data. We close this gap with CIGAsk , a recipe that pairs two reward signals inside a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) grades each clarification by comparing the gold-answer likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response; the resulting log-ratio is the per-turn reward at the corresponding clarification token. Anchoring the score to a frozen model decouples the credit signal from the actor being optimized, so the reward does not drift as the actor changes, as it can in policy-coupled information-gain variants (§ 2 ). The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a terminal bonus of + ρ +\rho , − ρ -\rho , or 0 0 based on the ambiguity label and whether the rollout asks for clarification, with no positive bonus merely for not requesting clarification on a clear query. A token-level two-stream advantage carries both signals through GRPO and reduces to vanilla GRPO when no rollout requests clarification (§ 3.2 ). Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce CIGAsk , pairing a per-turn frozen-reference reward (CIG) that grades how well each clarification elicits the missing fact with a terminal asymmetric bonus that gates when to ask. • We show that CIGAsk improves clarification performance across three benchmarks and transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning. It also preserves single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks without over-asking. 2 Related Work Multi-turn clarification and ambiguous QA. Two threads frame the problem. Benchmarks establish the under-specification regime: AmbigQA ( Min et al., 2020 ) , AbgCoQA ( Guo et al., 2021 ) , PACIFIC ( Deng et al., 2022 ) , ClariQ ( Aliannejadi et al., 2020 ) , QuestBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) ; adjacent multi-answer disambiguation ( Stelmakh et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2023 ) treats the same ambiguity from the answer side rather than the question side. Question-generation methods predate LLM agents and span EVPI ranking ( Rao and III, 2018 ) , conversational search ( Aliannejadi et al., 2019 ; Aliannejadi et al., 2020 ) , and expected-information-gain criteria ( Mazzaccara et al., 2024 ) ; they target how to ask while when is assumed externally. Training agents to clarify. Several lines of work train agents to clarify, differing in supervision regime. ACT ( Chen et al., 2025 ) pairs DPO-style action-level contrastive preferences with a Zephyr-7B base but does not score per-turn information value during training. AskBench ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) uses rubric-guided RLVR; Zhang et al. (2025) relabel RLHF preferences via simulated future turns but yield a binary signal; Suri et al. (2025) apply EVPI inside a fixed tool-call schema. Privileged-critic methods such as SWEET-RL ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) train a separately learned critic with ground-truth access at training time, but the critic is unavailable at deployment. Most similar in supervision is STaR-GATE ( Andukuri et al., 2024 ) , which self-trains on clarification trajectories filtered by outcome reward without per-turn credit; we differ precisely by the per-turn signal that decides which clarification surfaced the disambiguating fact. Outcome-only multi-turn RL recipes such as UserRL ( Qian et al., 2025 ) treat clarification as an opaque sub-trajectory. Per-turn credit assignment. Process reward models supply per-step credit but typically require step-labelled data: Math-Shepherd ( Wang et al., 2024 ) synthesises labels via Monte Carlo, VinePPO ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) via rollout trees, ImplicitPRM ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) via outcome-derived logits. Sullivan (2025) show vanilla GRPO with outcome reward equals a Monte-Carlo PRM only when group rollouts share identical prefixes, a condition multi-turn clarification rarely satisfies. Concurrent agentic variants assign turn-level credit via outcome propagation ( Wei et al., 2025 ) or trajectory-DPO-derived implicit step rewards ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , but compute the signal under the training policy and inherit the same collapse risk. Closest to our signal are two concurrent per-turn IG recipes. IGPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) computes turn-level rewards as the marginal increase in the training policy ’s probability of the correct answer for search agents; InfoPO ( Kong et al., 2026 ) computes the per-turn reward as the change in the agent ’s action distribution after user feedback for general user-centric agents. Neither uses a frozen reference: both score IG under the training policy itself, so the per-turn signal drifts as the actor updates, inheriting the degeneracy diagnosed by Setlur et al. (2025) . Neither pairs the per-turn signal with a label-driven gate on when to ask. Our frozen-reference formulation (§ 3.2 ) decouples credit from the actor and targets proactive clarification specifically rather than search or generic collaboration. Information-theoretic and counterfactual rewards originate in active learning ( MacKay, 1992 ) and curiosity-driven exploration ( Pathak et al., 2017 ) ; our self-supervised process reward sits in this family but consumes only the outcome-level gold answer. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries Multi-turn clarification setup. We formulate clarification as a POMDP with hidden state q ∗ q^{*} (the user’s true intent). At turn t t the agent observes history h < t = { ( a 1 , u 1 ) , … , ( a t − 1 , u t − 1 ) } h_{<t}{=}\{(a_{1},u_{1}),\ldots,(a_{t-1},u_{t-1})\} , context c c , and ambiguous question q q , then picks an action from 𝒜 = { Think , Clarify , Answer } \mathcal{A}{=}\{\textsc{Think},\textsc{Clarify},\textsc{Answer}\} : Think runs internal reasoning; Clarify emits a question that triggers a user response u t ∼ Sim ( ⋅ ∣ q ∗ , c , h < t ) u_{t}\!\sim\!\text{Sim}(\cdot\mid q^{*},c,h_{<t}) from a fixed simulator; Answer emits y ^ \hat{y} and terminates, after which y ^ \hat{y} is scored against gold y ∗ ∈ 𝒴 ∗ y^{*}\!\in\!\mathcal{Y}^{*} . The policy conditions on observable history rather than maintaining an explicit belief over q ∗ q^{*} ; the per-turn reward defined in § 3.2 supplies the supervision in its place. GRPO.
